passages.title: Indus Valley Civilization
passages.text:
Along with Egypt and Sumer, the third major early Bronze Age civilization was the Indus Valley civilization, which flourished from 2600 B.C. to 900 B.C. In geographic size, the Indus Valley civilization was the largest ancient urban civilization, bigger than pharaonic Egypt. Centered on the Indus River and the now dry Ghaggar-Hakra River, it comprised about 1,400 settlements across what is now Pakistan, Afghanistan, and northwestern India. The Indus Valley civilization was long considered archaeologically uninteresting because of its ordinary urban architecture and lack of palaces or citadels, but recent excavations show the civilization to be without parallel in history, displaying characteristics not elsewhere united in a single civilization.

The Indus Valley people, masters of urban planning, built brick cities on flood-proof terraces with grids of long, straight streets and the first urban sewer systems, made of masonry. No signs of dominant rulers have been found, and the cities’ living quarters show little sign of class distinction, suggesting that their system of government was, at least in part, democratic. The civilization also apparently thrived without armies—there is, for example, no evidence of weapon production.

The Indus Valley people were the first to cultivate rice and cotton, and they developed a carefully organized agricultural system to produce and distribute food. In addition, the Indus Valley civilization was one of the ancient world’s top traders. Examples of its standardized weights have been found in many harbors around the Arabian Sea, and Sumerian tablets inscribed in 2300 B.C. provide evidence that the Indus Valley people maintained trade with Mesopotamia.

The causes of the civilization’s decline, however, are not certain, and this has produced the most contention among scholars. A long-standing theory, one that today still inhabits history books, was proposed by British archaeologist Mortimer Wheeler in the 1920s and points to a final massacre by marauding Indo-Aryan invaders. But, in addition to a lack of written evidence of such an event in any ancient Indian records, there is no archaeological evidence of battles within the cities. In fact, new excavations show that Indo-Aryans were not even in the region at the time the massacre was alleged to have taken place. Archaeological evidence also shows a later resurgence of the civilization a substantial distance to the south of its original location. This suggests that the Indus Valley people most likely relocated for catastrophic environmental reasons, with the large empire disintegrating into many regional cultures. Severe drought, of which there is evidence, may have made some lands unfarmable. Without enough grain to feed the large urban populations, many of the Indus Valley civilization’s large cities would probably have been abandoned. Or, a massive earthquake in this seismically volatile region may have changed the course of rivers and disrupted many cities, spurring a migration of refugees to the countryside.

summaries.standard:
****Topic****

Indus Valley civilization

****Framework****

Highlight Something Noteworthy

****Main Point****

Recent excavations reveal an unusual combination of achievements in the Indus Valley civilization and undermine the old invasion account of its decline, suggesting environmental alternatives.

****Summary****

*P1 - Intro & Thesis*

The first two sentences give us our background info on the Indus Valley civilization (IVC). Then the final sentence of the paragraph gives us our primary big picture clues: *long considered boring, **but recent** is making us think it's really quite fascinating*.

As we read the rest of the passage, we'll assume we've already heard the main point, and we're really just hoping to grab a couple bullet points of subsidiary details.

*P2 - IVC had clever, modest, peaceful cities*

Their cities were laid out very logically. They had the first sewer system. They didn't seem to have rulers or much class distinction or much need for weapon production.

*P3 - IVC was good at agriculture and trade*

They were the first to grow rice and cotton, and they were avid traders.

*P4 - Possible causes for the decline of IVC*

The author considers a *long-standing* theory (hint-hint, author will probably disagree) that IVC was brought down by an invasion of Indo-Aryan invaders.

The author then debunks this theory and speculates some climate-environment-natural disaster alternatives.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.text: Recent evidence sheds new light on the Indus Valley civilization and calls into question some of the views held previously by archaeologists regarding its significance and decline.
Bronze Age civilizations, including that of the Indus Valley, have not been properly recognized for their cultural achievements.
The Indus Valley civilization played an important role in the evolution of democracy and modern agriculture.
The Indus Valley civilization is a historically significant culture, but there is not enough evidence to draw legitimate conclusions about the cultural practices of its people.
Certain long-held assumptions about the decline of the Indus Valley civilization exemplify how scholars can be led to incorrect conclusions by incomplete data.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following is NOT cited in the passage as a characteristic of the Indus Valley civilization?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Since the whole passage was about the IVC, it wouldn't be realistic to pre-game which details they'll be asking about.

We'll have to just prove to ourselves four answers that we know were said, unless we find a really obvious unsupported idea as our correct answer.

choices.text: It was geographically the largest of the major Bronze Age civilizations.
choices.explanation:
We've got an extreme-word alert: ****geographically largest****.

We can easily CTRL-F to find Bronze Age or just scan for those capital letters. We'll find it in the first two sentences, and indeed the IVC was *the largest*.

choices.text: Its people cultivated rice.
choices.explanation: We've got this detail in the beginning of the 3rd paragraph.

choices.text: Its people were generally nomadic.
choices.explanation: Do a CTRL-F for nomadic and ye shall not find it. To the contrary, the idea of an urbanized civilization, living off of agriculture, suggests the opposite of a nomadic civilization.

choices.text: It was a major trader.
choices.explanation: We learn this in the middle of the third paragraph.

choices.text: It was spread across an area that is now part of three nations.
choices.explanation: This is covered at the end of the first paragraph.

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, which one of the following most accurately describes the author's stance regarding Wheeler's theory?

choices.text: enthusiastic appreciation of its contributions to the field of archaeology
grudging approval of those aspects of the theory that have not been refuted by recent research
slight disagreement with its assumptions, mixed with respect for its venerable status
offhanded dismissal of it as a theory not worthy of scholarly attention
unambiguous rejection of it in light of newly conducted excavations

questions.prompt: Which one of the following is cited in the passage as evidence that directly counters Wheeler's theory?

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
Wheeler isn't brought up until the final paragraph, and even there he's only discussed in the first couple sentences.

Since we have such a *Defined Target*, we should definitely consider a Research-First approach.

What does the passage identify as evidence that goes against Wheeler?

We're told about Wheeler's theory in the second sentence of the final paragraph, and then we see the pushback:

*But, in addition to a lack of written evidence of such an event in any ancient Indian records, there is no archaeological evidence of battles within the cities. In fact, new excavations show Indo-Aryans weren't even in the region at the time of the alleged massacre.*

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
It looks like we have three possible answers:

- a lack of written evidence in any ancient Indian records that there was any massacre by marauding Aryans.

- no archaeological evidence of battles within the cities

- Indo-Aryans weren't even in the region at the time of the alleged massacre

choices.text: The Indus Valley is a seismically volatile region.
choices.explanation: The three available answers we have, "no written evidence / no archaeological evidence / IA's weren't in region at the time" have nothing to do with whether or not the region is seismically volatile (prone to earthquakes).

choices.text: There are no findings that indicate battles within Bronze Age Indus Valley cities.
choices.explanation:
This matches the second of our available details:
"there is no archaeological evidence of battles within the cities"

Archaeological evidence would be like destroyed buildings, spearheads, forts, etc.

So saying "there are no findings that indicate battles" is saying, "When archaeologists go looking for evidence of battles in these cities, they don't find anything".

choices.text: There is evidence of severe drought in the Indus Valley at the time of the Bronze Age.
choices.explanation: The three available answers we have, "no written evidence / no archaeological evidence / IA's weren't even in region" have nothing to do with whether or not there was a drought.

choices.text: No signs of dominant rulers of the Indus Valley civilization have been found at excavation sites.
choices.explanation: The three available answers we have, "no written evidence / no archaeological evidence / IA's weren't even in region" have nothing to do with whether or not there are signs of dominant rulers, only whether there are signs of battles within the cities.

choices.text: The Indus Valley people practiced agriculture.
choices.explanation: The three available answers we have, "no written evidence / no archaeological evidence / IA's weren't even in region" have nothing to do with whether or not the people practiced agriculture.

questions.prompt: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Is there any part of this passage that sounds distinctly like the Author's voice?

Well, most of it sounds like the author's voice. We might get reinforcement of any of the things the author rattled off about how impressive the IVC was:

- unique combo of features
- really good at urban planning
- remarkably free of war, income inequality
- seemingly democratic in part

But the real *Author Opinion* part of the passage was the last paragraph, in which she rejected one causal hypothesis for the demise of the IVC and proposed some alternatives.

She is saying, "There is no good case to make for the idea that Indo-Aryans were responsible for the downfall of the IVC. It's more likely that they faced a catastrophic environmental factor, such as a bad drought or bad earthquake."

choices.text: Because the Indus Valley region is prone to earthquakes, it is most likely that an earthquake destroyed the Indus Valley civilization.
choices.explanation: This answer would be fine if it said "it is possible / plausible", but the author never elevates this hypothesis to the level of ****#1 most likely****.

choices.text: Only a disaster as catastrophic as an earthquake would have caused the demise of a civilization as sophisticated as the Indus Valley civilization.
choices.explanation:
The author is saying that the end of the IVC was *probably* due to a catastrophic environmental reason.

I don't know if the "drought" hypothesis counts as "a disaster as catastrophic as an earthquake", but the fact that the author isn't even saying it ****needs**** to be a catastrophic disaster, just that it ****most likely**** was that, is enough to get rid of this answer.

choices.text: Archaeologists’ understanding of the decline of the Indus Valley civilization would benefit from a search for signs of earthquake damage in its cities.
choices.explanation: Since the author thinks that a massive earthquake *may have been* the reason for the downfall of the IVC, and since the cause of the civilization's decline is still not certain, we can presume she would say "let's investigate the *drought* hypothesis more. Let's investigate the *earthquake* hypothesis more."

choices.text: The cities of the Indus Valley civilization should have been better prepared for the possibility of a major earthquake.
choices.explanation:
The author is never scolding the IVC for having not sufficiently prepared for an earthquake.

She's sympathetically thinking, "This IS a seismically volatile region, so I can see a big quake having messed things up."

choices.text: The demise of the Indus Valley civilization was most likely caused by the catastrophic alteration of the courses of its major rivers.
choices.explanation: This answer would be fine if it said "possibly / plausibly caused" by catastrophic alteration of rivers, but the author never elevates this hypothesis to the level of ****#1 most likely****.

questions.prompt: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements about archaeological investigations into the Indus Valley civilization?

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
The last sentence of the 1st paragraph is where we find the keyword "archaeological".

It was long considered "uninteresting because of its ordinary architecture and lack of fancy buildings, but recent excavations show it to be without parallel in history, displaying characteristics not elsewhere united in a single civilization".

Those characteristics are things like these:
- awesome urban planning
- not much evidence of class distinction (so pretty democratic)
- first to cultivate rice and cotton / good system of food distribution

The last paragraph covers the decline of the civilization, for which there is no clear consensus. But we see "archaeological" show up a couple more times:
- no evidence of battles within the cities
- the civilization seemed to move a good bit south of its original location and then had a resurgence

choices.text: Archaeological data on the civilization were controlled by a small group of scholars for many years, leading to unfounded conclusions.
choices.tag: Out of Scope: controlled by small group
choices.explanation: There's nothing in the passage that suggests that a small group of scholars for many years controlled all the data on the civilization.

choices.text: It is only in recent years that scholars have gathered evidence sufficient to enable them to reach credible conclusions regarding the civilization.
choices.explanation: The passage contrasts earlier dismissal and a long-standing decline theory with recent excavations establishing the civilization's unusual characteristics and undermining the invasion explanation. That is the support for recent evidence enabling credible conclusions. It does not imply every earlier observation was baseless or that the precise cause of decline is now known.

choices.text: The Sumerian tablets that provide evidence of trade with the civilization contain the only known references to the civilization in ancient written records.
choices.explanation: Just because Sumerian tablets are the only ancient written record *mentioned* in the passage doesn't mean that those tablets are the only known ancient written records.

choices.text: While an adequate amount of archaeological data on the civilization has existed for many decades, most of it has been misinterpreted.
choices.explanation:
We have nothing in the passage to justify this strong statement that **more than 50%** of the archaeological data that we've had for decades has been misinterpreted.

It's also a stretch to say that "an adequate amount of data" has existed for many decades, since the passage is stressing that this civilization has been largely ignored until recently.

choices.text: The most recent archaeological investigations into the civilization are part of a broader trend in archaeology to avoid overreliance on written evidence.
choices.explanation: There's nothing in the passage to support the idea that these recent excavations regarding the Indus Valley civilization are part of any *broader trend in archaeology* regarding overreliance on written evidence.

passages.title: David Bordwell
passages.text:
Film scholar David Bordwell refers to the years 1917–1960 as the classical era of filmmaking in Hollywood. Bordwell defines the era’s style as being governed by straightforward narrative considerations, i.e., the need to follow well-defined characters through a chronological sequence of events, or plot. The technical elements of filmmaking—camera movement, lighting, editing, and sound—are all employed to tell a realistic story, one in which the world of the story is self-sufficient and recognizably related to our own. Devices that draw attention to the film as film rather than to the story are avoided.

Within this definition, the musical films of the 1930s are anomalous in that they interrupt narrative to present musical performances only tangentially related to the plot. In one film directed by Busby Berkeley, for example, a scene begins with a shot of an audience watching a singer. The singer’s face then fills the screen—a natural enough transition—but this image soon dissolves into a fanciful sequence consisting of various aerial views of city life. Although the sequence illustrates the song being sung, it does not contribute to the story Berkeley tells between musical numbers. In such sequences, filmmaking techniques are used not to advance a narrative but as a respite from narrative; the people we see are not characters in a plot but rather are abstracted figures; editing and camera movement function not to help tell a story but to manipulate images into intricate patterns. Can the musical—in which such differently motivated and constructed sequences abut so closely—fit comfortably within Bordwell’s definition of the classical style?

Bordwell’s response is that the musical, no less than comedy or melodrama (two other staples of the classical era), evolved from popular live theater. The musical’s conventions, Bordwell argues, cue viewers to expect a different structure—alternating narrative scenes and self-contained performances—from that of other genres, a structure that audiences are prepared for and thus accept as “realistic.” But raising the issue of genre does not disguise the fact that Bordwell stretches the definition of the term “realism,” for there is still the problem exemplified in films such as Berkeley’s by the fact that the musical performances are not merely self-contained but self-absorbed—the selfish aesthetic of the interlude isn’t intended to advance the plot but instead to draw attention to its own artistic expertise. Even the viewer aware of the film’s genre cannot remain entirely unfazed by the break in the film’s “reality.” Bordwell too quickly dismisses the fact that watching a film is a perceptual act and not an academic exercise in pigeonholing genres. Because knowledge of genre is acquired, it would be worthwhile for scholars like Bordwell to first consider how viewers process cinematic images and eventually come to accept them as conventions before generalizing about the realism of certain film styles.

summaries.standard:
****Topic****

Bordwell's definition of Hollywood's "classical period", as it relates to musicals

****Framework****

Challenge a Position

****Main Point****

Bordwell's explanation of how musicals fit within the realism of the "classical style" is not fully satisfying.

****Summary****

*P1 - Introduction to Bordwell's "classical era"*

This paragraph neutrally introduces Bordwell's characterization of the *classical era* -- basically, it was a realistic style that was all about telling a conventional story and making you forget that you were watching a movie. Stuff was only done to serve the interest of the narrative, not to call your attention to the fact that you were watching a work of visual art.

*P2 - The Curious case of Musicals*

It's weird that we don't get our central topic until the beginning of the 2nd paragraph, but the adjective "anomalous" is meant to have the same effect as our typical Purpose Pivot (usually using words like "but, yet, however, recently"). When we start with background and then pivot into something that feels like, "But this thing is different ... ", then we know that this different thing is what the author really wants to focus on.

This paragraph explains how musicals offer quite a challenge to the *classical era* definition, given that they have wacky musical numbers throughout the movie that are anything but realistic and don't have any purpose in advancing the story. The author innocuously asks whether musicals can be included in under the umbrella of *classical era*.

*P3 - Bordwell's handling of "musicals" and the author's critique of that handling*

Bordwell says, "Sure musicals still count. Yes, they have crazy interludes, but it's realistic because audience members are used to seeing live musicals, which have musical numbers, so audiences consider random, detached musical numbers as 'realistic' within the world of a musical."

The author ain't happy with this. She thinks it's really dodging the common sense issue that these musical numbers are totally un-realistic, and it also bothers the author that, as a viewer, you can plainly tell that the director is now just having fun as a visual artist, wants you to notice that, and doesn't any longer care about advancing the story.

The author is basically saying that even if an audience member said to themselves ahead of time, "This is a musical, so adjust expectations accordingly for this genre", the viewer would still notice the musical numbers as being a total break from reality.

The author concludes by trying to redirect the efforts of people like Bordwell so that they don't come back with crap they're currently selling, sayin' that musicals are realistic when they clearly aren't.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The central topic of the passage is how musical films of the 1930s connect with Bordwell's definition of the "classical era of filmmaking".

Why is the author writing about this? What was her purpose? What framework did we use?

By the end of the passage, we probably switched into a *Challenge Position* framework, because the author ends up spending most of the final paragraph pushing back against Bordwell's thinking:

- Bordwell stretches the definition
- there is still the problem
- Bordwell too quickly dismisses the fact
- it would be worthwhile for scholars like Bordwell to first consider

So we want our main point to sound like the author's central gripe with Bordwell.

She is saying that Bordwell's attempt to include musicals as part of the classical era is super fishy. Bordwell is saying that, even though a musical has parts that are obviously not realistic, people accept spontaneous song-and-dance numbers as part of the reality of the world of musicals.

Our author thinks Bordwell is really stretching reality to make this work and recommending that instead of thinking that "genre defines how an audience member experiences the realism of a work" we should instead be thinking "how does an audience member's experience later allow them to talk about genre".

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Look for an answer saying something like, "Bordwell's attempt to include musicals in the classical era is super fishy".

choices.text: Despite some evidence to the contrary, Bordwell’s definition of the classical style of filmmaking is borne out by a more careful examination of Hollywood film genres such as the musical.
choices.explanation: This answer is saying that Bordwell's examination of musicals lends ****credence**** to his definition of the classical era. This answer not only sound complimentary of Bordwell (whereas we're seeking more of a *Challenge Position* vibe), but it also makes musicals sound like a great illustration of the classical style, when the passage is portraying them as a very poor fit.

choices.text: Contrary to Bordwell’s claims, the musicals of the 1930s such as Busby Berkeley’s are not realistic because they do not depict events in chronological order.
choices.explanation:
This answer makes it seem like the central question was "given that musicals of the 1930s don't depict events in chronological order, can we really consider them realistic?"

That's not too far off, but the central question was more, "given that musicals of the 1930s aren't realistic (because they contain fanciful interludes that have nothing to do with advancing the story), can we really consider them part of the classical era?"

Also, it's completely out of scope to claim that musicals don't depict events in chronological order. The passage never said or suggested that.

choices.text: Because film genres such as the musical evolved from popular theatrical forms, it can be argued that they fit comfortably within Bordwell’s definition of the classical style of filmmaking.
choices.explanation:
The main clause here is saying that musicals ****do**** fit comfortably within Bordwell's definition, and the author's main point is to argue that they don't.

Bordwell tries to justify including them under that definition and the author thinks his justification is whack.

choices.text: The films of Busby Berkeley do not meet the requirements of Bordwell’s definition of the classical style of filmmaking and therefore cannot be considered examples of the classical style of filmmaking.
choices.explanation: This answer portrays the central topic of the passage as "the films of Busby Berkeley". He was just an example, not a main topic.

choices.text: The fact that Bordwell’s definition of the classical style of filmmaking is obliged to treat musicals of the 1930s as realistic, despite compelling evidence to the contrary, illustrates the misguided nature of Bordwell’s approach.
choices.explanation:
This has the *Challenge Position* vibe we wanted. The main clause is "X illustrates the misguided nature of Bordwell's approach".

The answer correctly captures the central topic: "do musicals of the 1930s really fit the definition of the classical era?"

And it captures the fact that Bordwell tried to argue that they do, and the author thought his justification was super fishy.

questions.prompt: The passage identifies each of the following as a component of Bordwell's definition of the classical style of filmmaking EXCEPT:

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body: It looks like there are a lot of descriptors in the first paragraph, so I would reacquaint myself with those and then go hunt for four matches in the answer.

choices.text: avoidance of filmmaking techniques that call attention to the film medium
choices.explanation: This appears at the end of the 1st paragraph.

choices.text: creation and presentation of clearly defined characters
choices.explanation: This is supported in the 2nd sentence.

choices.text: portrayal of a self-sufficient and relatively realistic world
choices.explanation: This appears in the 2nd to last sentence of the 1st paragraph.

choices.text: use of nonnarrative interludes between episodes of plot
choices.explanation:
This answer describes the funky characteristic of musicals that makes the author wonder why Bordwell is cool with including musicals as part of the classical style.

Bordwell ends up giving a weird explanation that, to someone who has seen musicals in live theater, it is a "realistic" expectation of that genre to have nonnarrative interludes between episodes of plot.

But excusing away the anomalous feature of musicals doesn't mean that Bordwell considers that anomalous feature to be a signature feature of the classical style. He considers it a tolerable exception that doesn't justify booting musicals out of this category.

This answer choice goes squarely against how Bordwell defines the classical era:
a nonnarrative interlude is the antithesis of *being governed by straightforward narrative considerations*.

choices.text: depiction of a chronological sequence of events
choices.explanation: This shows up in the second sentence.

questions.prompt: The author uses the term "realistic" throughout the passage to refer to which one of the following qualities of a film?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
In the first paragraph the author seems to define 'realistic story' as "one in which the world of the story is self-sufficient and recognizably related to our own. Devices that draw attention away from the story (and to the awareness that you're seeing a film) are avoided."

Musicals are seen by the author as lacking this realistic quality, since there are gigantic song and dance numbers that would never happen in real life and that presumably remind you that you're seeing a musical, rather than keeping you immersed in the realistic story.

Bordwell tries to argue that audiences who see musicals accept the fact that people occasionally break into song and dance as a "realistic" feature of the self-contained world of musicals.

But the author thinks that he is ****stretching**** the definition of realism. She could tolerate the idea of musical numbers that add a layer of song and dance atop the story and characters of the basic plot. But she thinks that when you get into "self-absorbed" territory, like Disney's *Fantasia* or the Berkeley film, you get into this experimental visual realm that is making the viewer think about the visuals rather than think about the story.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
It seems like the author is treating "realism" as whether or not the action on the screen is fundamentally still related to the characters and the story. Once the action on screen is visuals for the sake of itself, "look at these pretty images", then you've taken the audience out of the 'realistic' mode of following the progression of a narrative.

So let's look for something like "the world of the story is self-sufficient, recognizably related to our won, and doesn't take detours that draw attention away from the story".

choices.text: the quality that allows the narrative structure to convey the story being told in the film
choices.explanation:
This answer is kind of tempting because it's emphasizing the narrative and the story, which is definitely something the author is associating with realism.

But this idea that there is "a quality that ****allows**** the narrative structure to convey the story" reads like artsy-fartsy nonsense.

We would probably be wise to keep this on a first pass, since it's not easy to pinpoint why it's wrong, but it's way harder to support this confusing language than it is to support the correct answer. The quality of a film that allows the narrative structure to convey the story would presumably be stuff like *plot, dialogue, action*?

choices.text: the quality that allows the world of the story told in the film to resemble actual life
choices.explanation:
This is very supportable based on the 3rd sentence of the passage, where the author defines 'a realistic story' as "one in which the world of the story is recognizably related to our own".

This answer almost matches up word for word.

It's a little frustrating that the question stem emphasizes how 'realism' is used throughout the passage, and it seems like the term takes on other flavors of meaning in the 3rd paragraph, none of which are captured here. But ultimately, it's hard to not consider this the best available answer when it sounds just like the way the author defines realism in the first paragraph.

choices.text: the quality that allows the technical elements of filmmaking to contribute to the story being told in the film
choices.explanation:
The 3rd sentence of the passage says that the technical elements are employed to tell a realistic story.

This answer is saying that realism is employed to allow the technical elements to contribute to the story.

So it seems to be reversing the stated flow of causality. We use the technical stuff to hep achieve realism, whereas this says that we use realism to help empower the technical elements.

choices.text: the quality that allows audiences to determine easily the genre to which the film belongs
choices.explanation:
The author never makes it seem like "realism" is a tool that allows the audience to determine the genre.

The 3rd paragraph at one point says that "even the viewer aware of the film's genre cannot be unfazed by the break in 'reality'."

This suggests that awareness of genre exists independently of whether realism is present.

choices.text: the quality that allows the film to employ a variety of narrative structures to tell a story
choices.tag: Out of Scope: variety of structures
choices.explanation: The passage does not define realism as enabling a variety of narrative structures. The explicit definition concerns a story world self-sufficient and recognizably related to our own, making B the direct match. Similar wording among other answers does not make them cancel one another out.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Generally speaking, these Organization answers devote about one ingredient per paragraph. Usually, the quickest way to find out an answer is wrong is by looking at its final ingredient.

P1 - introduce a scholar's definition of a certain time period/style

P2 - discussion of a particular group that doesn't seem to fit definition

P3 - scholar's response / author's evaluation of that response

choices.text: The author states a scholar’s thesis, counters the thesis with an example, summarizes the scholar’s response to the example, points out a problem with the response, and criticizes the focus of the scholar’s research.
choices.explanation:
The last three ingredients here all come from the last paragraph, making this answer seem a little weird, but everything is accurate.

The author state's Bordwell's thesis in the 1st paragraph, counters it in the 2nd paragraph with the example of musicals, summarizes Bordwell's response to the musical 'counterexample' in the beginning of the 3rd, and then the author shoots down the response and recommends an alternate research direction.

The "But raising the issue of genre" part of the 3rd paragraph is where the author is pointing out her problem with Bordwell's response, and the final sentence is where the author is implicitly 'criticizing' the scholar's research by saying "what they *really should* be doing is ____ ".

choices.text: The author takes issue with a scholar’s thesis, provides an example in support of a counterthesis, summarizes the scholar’s response to the example, and argues in favor of replacing the scholar’s thesis with the counterthesis.
choices.explanation:
This lacks a match for the first paragraph, so it looks like a good idea to bail early. The passage starts with a paragraph of Bordwell, not with the author taking issue with something.

We would also find mismatches in terms of "counterthesis" (this doesn't happen -- it would sound like our author saying, "No, Bordwell, the *real* definition of the Classical style is ____ "), and thus we also couldn't say that at the end the author wants to replace Bordwell's thesis with a counterthesis.

choices.text: The author states a scholar’s thesis, illustrates the thesis with an example, summarizes the scholar’s interpretation of the example, points out a problem with the interpretation, and makes a suggestion for modifying the interpretation.
choices.explanation:
This is super close to being correct (and super close to resembling choice A), but the example of "musical films" is not meant to illustrate the thesis.

It's meant to be a challenge to the thesis. The scholar doesn't interpret the example ... the scholar defends his thesis against the challenge.

choices.text: The author takes issue with a scholar’s thesis, provides an example illustrating the drawbacks of the thesis, summarizes the scholar’s response to the example, points out a problem with the response, and offers a new thesis to replace the scholar’s thesis.
choices.explanation:
This lacks a match for the first paragraph, so it looks like a good idea to bail early. The passage starts with a paragraph of Bordwell, not with the author taking issue with something.

The last ingredient is also awry. The author doesn't offer a new thesis to replace the scholar's; she just proposes a better direction for future inquiry.

choices.text: The author states a scholar’s thesis, presents the results of research supporting the thesis, counters the results with an example, summarizes the scholar’s response to the example, acknowledges the legitimacy of the response, but suggests that further research is needed to settle the matter.
choices.explanation:
We do indeed start with a scholar's thesis, but we don't present the results of any *research* (and the 2nd paragraph is challenging the thesis, not supporting it).

We can stop reading there.

It is funny, though, to see "acknowledges the legitimacy of the response", since our author does ****not**** think Bordwell's defense of why musical films are included is a legit response.

questions.prompt: The author of the passage would most likely agree with which one of the following statements?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
There's not much to go off from the question stem, but we know that the majority of the author's tone / opinion came in the latter half of the final paragraph.

We might expect the answer to reinforce some of the author's main sentiments:
- you can't call musicals 'realistic' even if people expect random musical numbers in that genre

- the fact that the musical numbers are so artistically ambitious makes you think about the director / cinematographer who are proud of themselves for their visual art, rather than think about the story of the film

- you should realize that viewers aren't sitting down deciding on genre ahead of time, but rather perceiving a movie and maybe coming to genre conclusions later

- Bordwell and his ilk should be focusing more on how viewer process films in realtime and later come to accept certain things as conventions of a genre

Mostly, though, we want to just be wary of language that seems Too Strong/Specific, Unknown Comparisons, Out of Scope, or Wrong Point of View (like Bordwell's)

choices.text: Busby Berkeley’s films are unique among musicals in that their performance sequences do not contribute to their narratives.
choices.explanation:
The author is thinking that Berkeley's musicals are not unique but rather indicative of musicals of that era.

In the beginning of the second paragraph, she talks about "the musical films of the 1930s" and then in the following sentence says, "In one film by Berkeley, ****for example ..."**** indicating that it is illustrative of musical films of the 30s.

choices.text: The use of technical elements in films of the classical era was usually very simplistic.
choices.explanation:
One problem in interpreting this answer is that our author doesn't really love that musicals are being filed under "classical era", so can we count them among "films of the classical era"?

In this passage, the musicals are included, and they definitely involve some complex stuff. Towards the end of the 2nd paragraph it says that, "editing and camera movement function not to help tell a story but to manipulate images into ****intricate**** patterns".

Even if we left out the negative support that musicals provide for this answer, though, we still wouldn't find any positive support for this answer as it pertains to non-musicals.

Nothing in the first paragraph means anything like "usually ****very**** simplistic".

choices.text: The film genres popular in the classical era were all derived from noncinematic popular entertainment forms.
choices.explanation: Bordwell connects three named genres, musical, comedy and melodrama, with live theater. Calling them staples does not establish that all popular genres, or all classical-era genres, had that origin.

choices.text: Audiences learn to accept certain cinematic images as conventions primarily through repeated exposure to such images.
choices.explanation:
This comes from the final sentence of the passage:
*viewers process cinematic images and* *****eventually***** *(repeated exposure) come to accept them as conventions.*

The word "primarily" is definitely a red flag word, but in context it feels pretty fair.

The author is stressing, right before this line, that "knowledge of genre is ****acquired****", and then says we should be studying ****how**** viewers process images and eventually accept them as conventions.

So that context makes it seem like our author thinks this process is central to knowledge of genre is acquired.

choices.text: Most musical films of the 1930s concentrated on telling realistic stories.
choices.explanation: The author discusses narrative interruptions and the problem of treating their performance sequences as realistic. The passage gives no proportion of musicals concentrated on realistic stories overall. Criticism of the interludes does not establish the opposite claim about the realism of every surrounding plot.

questions.prompt: The narrative structure of which one of the following hypothetical novels is most closely parallel to that of the musical films of the 1930s, as that genre is described by the author of the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Supporting Text
explanationBlocks.body:
We get some description of 1930s musicals in the beginning of the 2nd paragraph:
*they interrupt narrative to present musical performances only tangentially related to the plot*

As the paragraph continues, we learn that these musical performances are kind of just like artsy music videos, like if you were watching an episode of "Game of Thrones", but then for 3 minutes it was just a music video of dudes riding horses through the snow. Moody? Sure. Artistic? Sure.

But it's not actually related to the story.

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body: So we want something that takes diversions / interruptions / detours from the main story to provide a weird standalone "music video". In the case of a novel, I guess it would just be a moody, artistic passage of prose that didn't actually have much of anything to do with advancing the story.

choices.text: a novel that depicts a series of events, moving from one event to another without providing information necessary for understanding the context or chronology of the events
choices.explanation:
We do get a series of events (i.e. a story), but it's not saying there are periodic interludes of fanciful artistry. It's just saying that it's not connected well. The series of events doesn't provide meaningful connective tissue.

In the musical films, the story has connective tissue, it's just we "take 5" from the story every now and then to be weird.

choices.text: a novel that follows a number of characters who do not know one another, depicting a single event in each of their lives and concluding with a final event that unites all of the characters
choices.explanation: This doesn't have any gaps in the story where the book just gets weird.

choices.text: a novel that follows a number of characters who all reside in the same town, depicting a single event in each of their lives that together combine to form a portrait of a typical day in the town
choices.explanation:
This sounds a lot like (B) ... a bunch of separate vignettes that tie together in the end.

Separate vignettes is not quite the same as periodic interludes.

We weren't being told that in musical films, the audience is following four or five different storylines that all converge toward the end. We were told that they are following ONE main story, but that several times during the film, we have a gratuitous music video.

choices.text: a novel that follows a protagonist through a series of events, pausing throughout to provide information relevant to the events by means of fanciful flashbacks to the protagonist’s youth
choices.explanation:
This is very close. *Pausing throughout for fanciful flashbacks* is exactly what we're looking for, but they're supposed to be tangential to the story (not helping with the story).

Unfortunately, this one says that the flashbacks *provide information relevant to the events*, so these interludes actually ****do**** help move the story along.

choices.text: a novel that follows a protagonist through the events of a single day, pausing throughout for stylistically elaborate sections expressing the protagonist’s thoughts and fantasies about life in general
choices.explanation:
*Pausing throughout for stylistically elaborate sections* is similar to having random musical numbers sprinkled throughout.

They're supposed to be tangential to the story, and this answer establishes that the story is about a single day, but these interludes are about thoughts and fantasies about life in general, so not integral to understanding the story of that day.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, would most call into question the position of Bordwell described in the first two sentences of the last paragraph?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
What is Bordwell's position in those first two sentences of the last paragraph?

He's saying that the musical evolved from popular live theater, and that the musical's conventions cue viewers to expect a different structure from that of other genres (one that tolerates periodic breaks from the plot to have a musical number); audiences are prepared for this structure and thus accept it as "realistic".

We could potentially weaken this idea by contradicting any of its claims or assumptions
- the musical did not evolve from popular live theater
- the musical's conventions due not cue viewers to expect its wacky structure
- audiences are not prepared for its structure
- being prepared for a wacky structure does not mean that you accept it as "realistic"

choices.text: evidence that reviewers of musical films in the 1930s generally praised the films’ unrealistic elements
choices.explanation: Bordwell's position in those two sentences is about audiences, not reviewers, so anything we learn about reviewers will be a stretch to connect to his position on audiences.

choices.text: evidence that audiences went to musical films in the 1930s primarily to enjoy the musical performances
choices.explanation: This seems to gel fine with Bordwell's comments. He thinks audience members know musicals from live theater and accept its frequent musical performances. This answer just adds, "Not only do they accept them, that's the main draw!"

choices.text: evidence that viewers of musical films in the 1930s all experienced these films in the same way, whether or not they had previously been exposed to musicals
choices.explanation:
Bordwell's position in those first two sentences is that "*because of* having seen musicals in popular live theater, audiences who see musicals in a film are cued to expect the different structure of musicals and thus they accept random musical numbers as 'realistic' within the universe of the musical."

This is a No Cause, Effect type of causality weakener.

If people who haven't seen musicals in live theater are experiencing musical films the same way as people who *have* seen musicals in live theater, then Bordwell seems wrong to think that the latter group has been changed / cued to have different expectations and thus different experiences.

choices.text: evidence that audience members tend to have longer attention spans when watching films with whose genres they are unfamiliar
choices.explanation:
It's pretty hard to connect this totally vague answer to musicals vs. other films, or to the 1930s vs. other eras.

"Attention span" in general is a pretty out of scope concept for the entire passage.

choices.text: evidence that the musicals presented in popular live theater before the 1930s are stylistically very similar to the musical films of the 1930s
choices.explanation:
We could have weakened by saying, "Yeah, but Bordwell, musical *films* are way different from musicals performed in live theater, so the expectations that audiences learned from live theater aren't going to be matched by what they see in a musical film."

But this answer does the opposite, making the two things more fair to compare.

passages.title: The Concept of Blame
passages.text:
**Passage A**

The legal system rests on the assumption that people use conscious deliberation when deciding how to act—that is, in the absence of external duress, people freely decide how to act. But behaviors—even high-level behaviors—can take place in the absence of free will. For example, someone with a neurological disorder might form a facial expression without *choosing* to do so.

The crucial legal question is whether *all* of our actions are fundamentally beyond our control or whether some little bit of you is “free” to choose, independent of the rules of biology. After all, as neurologists tell us, there is no spot in the brain that is not densely interconnected with—and driven by—other brain parts. And that suggests that no part is independent and therefore "free."

One thing seems clear: if free will *does* exist, it has little room in which to operate. It can at best be a small factor riding on top of vast neural networks shaped by genes and environment. In fact, free will may end up being so small that we eventually think about bad decision-making in the same way we think about any physical affliction.

Blameworthiness should thus be removed from the legal argot. It is a backward-looking concept that demands the impossible task of untangling the hopelessly complex web of genetics and environment in order to isolate a factor of free will that may or may not exist. Instead of debating culpability, the legal system has to become forward looking, and address how an accused lawbreaker is likely to behave in the future.

**Passage B**

Here is a paradox: if people lack free will, then how can the law be moved away from what seems to be a deeply entrenched reliance on blame-related concepts? Rational arguments will only get you so far.

Clinical research indicates that people will often continue to make moral judgments even when they are conditioned to think that human behavior is determined by physical processes. The blaming urge is deeply rooted in the human psyche, and I have considerable doubt that any amount of scientific evidence can remove it from our criminal justice processes.

We have, of course, tried this before. Rehabilitation was widely accepted by criminal justice experts in the mid-twentieth century. But public support waned, and a retributive backlash occurred in the 1970s and 1980s. Criminal behavior may be a matter of biology, not choice, but the public seems unwilling to incorporate this idea into the law.

My sense is that blaming performs some useful social function, even if it is in some way “false.” Blaming seems too intrinsically a part of the social life of human beings for me to see it as a worthless appendage that can be harmlessly amputated. As the criminal justice system confronts the challenges of brain science, it should also seek a better understanding of why people blame and try to continue to respect the underlying social needs.

summaries.standard:
****Passage A****

The main takeaway from this passage is the first sentence of last paragraph: let's get rid of "blame" as a part of the legal vocabulary.

How did we get there?

The legal system rests on an assumption of free will, but we're also aware that behavior often takes place in the absence of free will.

So the crucial legal question becomes -- how much of our behavior is truly free? The dense interconnection of brain parts suggests that no part is independently free. The author isn't ready to say "none", but she admits in the 3rd paragraph that it's probably only a tiny sliver of our behavior.

Since we don't want court cases to become impossible arguments over whether the defendant's behavior came from a rare bit of free will or from a lifetime of genetic / environmental influences, we should stop trying to debate blame and should just think about how we avert bad behavior in the future.

****Passage B****

This passage is essentially a continuation of Passage A --- "Even granting the possibility that free will is absent, can rational arguments remove blame from the law, and would removing it disregard useful social functions?"

The idea that '****rational**** arguments will only get you so far' is foreshadowing the author's argument that there is some ****emotional/instinctive**** component to blame that we won't be able to shed:
- blaming urge deeply rooted in our psyche
- we tried rehabilitation instead of retribution before, and retribution made a comeback.
- there seems to be some social function played by blaming, and so the criminal justice system needs to reckon with that as it considers getting rid of "blame" as a concept.

****Similarities****

Both passages are discussing blame, the legal system, free will, rehab vs. punishment.

****Differences****

Passage A is arguing we should get rid of "blame". Passage B is arguing, "maybe we *should*, but I doubt we *can*. We should grapple with why people feel such a consistent urge to blame."

questions.prompt: Both passages are primarily concerned with answering which one of the following questions?

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
The main point of Passage A can be found in the first sentence of its last paragraph.

After all, it has both a "should" (prescriptive opinion) and a "thus" (drawing a conclusion).

The author has spent the first few paragraphs establishing a problem in law: our laws and punishments assume that rational actors are freely choosing their actions, but neurology suggests that most, if not all, of our mental activity is not coming from free will.

What's the author's solution to this problem?

Let's stop "blaming" people as though they could have done otherwise but purposefully made a *wrong* choice. Let's accept that most, if not all, behavior is the product of complex background factors and rather than worrying about who to blame, just think about how the ingredients that went into *this* offense could be thwarted in the future.

Passage B is also talking about free will and blame, as early as the first sentence.

Given that both passages overlap in terms of their central topic, we should except the correct answer to this question to be posing some question about blame / free will.

Passage B's second and fourth paragraphs continue to talk about "blame", whereas free will is not discussed throughout.

So then let's say that **blame** is definitely the central crux of both passages. The author of B doesn't want to get rid of blame, because she's pretty sure it's an important part of our social DNA.

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body: Let's look for a question like, "Should we stop/keep blaming criminals for their crimes?"

choices.text: Does the public support rehabilitation over retribution as the purpose of criminal justice?
choices.explanation: Public support for rehabilitation is evidence in B's argument, but A focuses on whether blame belongs in the legal system. The answer selects a subsidiary issue that is not the primary shared question.

choices.text: Is the existence of free will compatible with the findings of brain science?
choices.explanation: A considers neurological reasons to doubt free will, but both passages use that issue to discuss the legal role of blame. B primarily considers feasibility and social function, not a full philosophical assessment of compatibility.

choices.text: Does the legal system require the assumption that people choose freely?
choices.explanation: A identifies a traditional assumption and B considers what follows if free will is absent. Their main focus is whether criminal justice should retain blame, rather than whether the legal system necessarily requires a free-will assumption. B's conditional discussion does not prove an unconditional commitment that free will is absent.

choices.text: Should the concept of blame be removed from criminal justice procedures?
choices.explanation:
Well they made this a little easier on us by only giving us one answer that dealt with "blame".

Passage A's main point is, "Yes, blame should be removed." That's the beginning of A's final paragraph.

Passage B's main point is, "No, blame should not be removed." That's the essence of B's final paragraph. He thinks that blame performs a useful social function that cannot be harmlessly amputated (i.e. to get rid of it would cause harm). He says we should "try to continue to respect the underlying social needs of people needing to blame others".

choices.text: Is criminal behavior comparable to a physical affliction?
choices.explanation:
Since this doesn't say "blame", which is the central topic of both passages and main points, we shouldn't be attracted to this answer on the first pass.

If we bothered to read it, we would see that it's discussing "physical afflictions", which was said in passing in Passage A and never said at all in Passage B.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately describes the attitude of the author of passage B toward the type of argument presented in passage A?

choices.text: sympathy with the premises, accompanied by doubts about the feasibility of the policy those premises are used to support.
intellectual acceptance, coupled with fear of the consequences if such acceptance becomes widespread
forceful rejection, both of the argument’s conclusion and one or more of the premises on which it is based
studied neutrality, with regard both to the conclusion and to the steps by which it is arrived at
sympathy with the conclusion amid doubt that it follows from the premises

questions.prompt: The meaning of the phrase "forward looking" (last sentence of passage A) as it is used in passage A is most closely related to which one of the following concepts in passage B?

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
In passage A, the final paragraph is saying "let's get rid of blame. That's all about looking into the past for whom to blame this crime on."

Instead, the author thinks we should look to the future: "regardless of how this crime happened; how can we keep it from happening again?"

Presumably, that would mean,
*instead of trying to figure out the right **punishment** for a wrongdoer (which means we have to correctly ascertain their level of blame / free will), we should just try to figure out the right **tactic** for helping this person avoid wrongdoing in the future.*

Maybe that's medicine / maybe that's rehabilitation / maybe that's better economic opportunities.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: So we want an answer that has to do with how we can "fix" a wrongdoer going forward so that they don't commit offenses in the future.

choices.text: entrenched
choices.explanation:
"Entrenched" was used to describe our relationship with the backwards-looking concept of blame.

"forward looking" is about trying to "fix" a wrongdoer going forward so that they don't commit offenses in the future.

choices.text: rational
choices.explanation:
The use of "rational" was to modify argument we might make against blaming people for things for which they may have no free will to change.

"Forward looking" is about trying to "fix" a wrongdoer going forward so that they don't commit offenses in the future.

choices.text: conditioned
choices.explanation: Conditioned describes subjects being led to think behavior is physically determined, despite which they often continue making moral judgments. It does not name the forward-looking treatment of an offender. Rehabilitation is the closer match.

choices.text: rehabilitation
choices.explanation:
"Forward looking" is about trying to "fix" a wrongdoer going forward so that they don't commit offenses in the future.

That's the goal of rehabilitation: to change someone for the better so that they cease their bad ways.

In passage B, it was saying that, "We've tried to get out of the blame game before. We tried the looking-forward approach. Rehabilitation was super popular in the mid-1900s."

choices.text: backlash
choices.explanation:
"Backlash" was used to describe how people felt about rehabilitation (which is forward-looking).

"Backlash" was people expressing their desire to blame and punish the wrongdoer.

questions.prompt: It is most likely that the authors of the passages would disagree with each other about the truth of which one of the following statements?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Since we're looking for what the authors would disagree about, we can ask ourselves where the two passages diverged.

Their overall main points were pretty divergent.

Passage A was saying, "Since we don't have free will (basically), we should probably get rid of the concept of blame from our legal system"

and Passage B was saying, "Even though we don't have free will, we probably can't get rid of the concept of blame from our legal system."

Let's look for something testing that big picture disagreement, and then pick any answer we think we can support by pointing to one author agreeing with it and the other disagreeing with it.

choices.text: A significant portion of people’s choices are made freely.
choices.explanation:
Passage B is sort of accepting out of the gate that we don't have free will, so he would disagree with this claim.

And Passage A would also disagree with this claim because it says "a ****significant**** portion" of choices are made freely. Passage A said that,

*One thing seems clear: if free will* *****does***** *exist, it has little room in which to operate. It can at best be a small factor ...*

choices.text: If free will does not exist, criminal law should not assign blame for any action.
choices.explanation:
This speaks to the difference in main points, as we anticipated. They just found a putrid way to word it, as is their talent.

Passage A concludes by saying that given that free will does not exist or barely exists, "blameworthiness should be removed from the legal argot" (from the legal vocabulary)

Passage B concludes with the author defending the idea that blame does still perform some useful social function. It can't be harmless amputated (it would harm us to get rid of the concept of blame). The criminal justice system "should seek a better understanding of why people blame and try to ****continue to**** respect the underlying social needs (continue to assign blame)."

choices.text: People should be imprisoned for actions from which they are not free to refrain.
choices.tag: Out of Scope: should be imprisoned
choices.explanation:
Neither author discussed anything in the realm of their thoughts on whether people should or shouldn't be imprisoned.

Even if you think people lack free will and shouldn't be blamed for a crime, you still might think they should be imprisoned because they're a danger to society, so we can't presume any leaps from the author's positions on blame to their potential positions on imprisonment.

choices.text: Actions that are completely determined by physical processes are not free.
choices.explanation:
This is a fishy answer for Passage B, which really didn't get into the nitty gritty of whether free will exists.

But by definition if an action is "****completely**** determined by physical processes" then we're not calling it free. So both authors would agree with this.

choices.text: It is easy to eliminate the concept of blame from everyday life.
choices.tag: Out of Scope Passage A: easy to eliminate
choices.explanation:
We know that Passage B would heartily disagree with this answer, but we couldn't support the idea that Passage A would argue, "It is ****easy**** to eliminate the concept of blame from everyday life".

Passage A says we *should* eliminate the concept from our legal vocabulary, but that doesn't mean it will be easy to do so, let alone outside the legal world in everyday life.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, would cast the most doubt on the argument in passage B?

choices.text: A new drug enables patients with a particular neurological disorder to exercise apparent control over their symptoms.
In patients with a particular brain injury, the two hemispheres of the brain become causally isolated from one another.
Subjects in a psychological experiment display random responses to a repeated stimulus.
Some governments restrict the legal concept of blame to cases of disobedience to the authorities.
There are societies that have no concept of blame.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following conforms to the policy advocated by the author of passage A but not advocated by the author of passage B?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Passage A's policy was, "Since we have little to no control over our actions, let's not blame people for their actions".

Passage B's policy was, "Since blame seems to have a really important role in our psyche / society, let's try to still respect that role."

So it seems like a policy conforming to A but not B would be one that is defiantly saying, "There is no blame!"

choices.text: Parents should refrain from words and actions that could cause their children to feel ashamed of behavior that the parents regard as socially unacceptable.
choices.explanation: This is more about socializing than blaming. Neither author was addressing whether parents should provide feedback to their children in the interest of editing / shaping their behavior going forward.

choices.text: Prosecutors should be allowed to exclude jurors whose beliefs about free will make them unwilling to assign blame to anyone who is accused of a crime.
choices.explanation:
This is so specific about jury selection rules that I would be scared to pick it no matter what, but on the face of this it sounds like the opposite of passage A.

Passage A was saying "blame has no place in the legal system".

This answer is saying, "any juror that thinks that blame has no place in the legal system should be disallowed."

choices.text: The admissibility of expert testimony regarding a defendant’s state of mind should be subject to strict guidelines.
choices.explanation: A rejects backward-looking culpability debates but does not specify guidelines for admitting expert testimony. Evidence about state of mind might also bear on future behavior. The answer is unsupported as A's policy, rather than clearly contradicted.

choices.text: The findings of brain science should be viewed with suspicion, since they imply that the brain scientists themselves did not arrive at them by conscious deliberation.
choices.explanation: The author of A is pretty trusting of the findings of brain science; after all, that's what is motivating him to say, "Since we have (almost) no free will, let's ditch the concept of blame."

choices.text: Courts should be allowed to consider a convicted criminal’s motives to determine the likelihood that the criminal will offend again, but not to determine degree of culpability.
choices.explanation:
This sounds a ton like Passage A's final sentence:
- we shouldn't debate culpability (i.e. blame)
- we should focus on thwarting future offenses

And since this answer says so defiantly, "Courts should ****not**** be allowed to determine degree of blame", it goes against the final sentence of Passage B, which thinks that the legal system still needs a way to "respect the underlying social need for blame".

passages.title: Carroll and Chen's Multiverse
passages.text:
Physicists posit that at first our universe was infinitesimally small and infinitely hot and dense. It then underwent a period of extremely rapid, massive inflation (the Big Bang), and it has since continued to expand and cool.

According to physicists Sean Carroll and Jennifer Chen, the Big Bang was not a unique event; events like it happen periodically over an incredibly vast time scale. This is based on the suggestion of some physicists that the Big Bang was the beginning of our universe as we know it, but not the beginning of a larger Universe—or “multiverse”—that encompasses everything, including that which we can never see because it is beyond our “cosmic bubble.”

Carroll and Chen were initially interested in why time flows in only one direction. In physics the flow of time is captured by the second law of thermodynamics, which implies that entropy—a measure of total disorder—naturally increases with time. Entropy increases because there are more ways for a system to be disordered than for it to be ordered. Therefore, if change occurs, it is more likely to be change toward greater disorder. For example, in a moderately orderly room, if one moves an object in the room randomly, there are many more places one can put it that will make the room less orderly than there are places that will make it more orderly. So if, over time, objects in the room are continually moved randomly, it is most likely that the room will get increasingly disordered.

While the Big Bang process and what followed obey the second law of thermodynamics, it is a mystery why there should have been a small, hot, and dense universe to begin with. Such a low entropy universe is an extremely unlikely configuration, not what scientists would expect from a randomly occurring initial condition. Carroll and Chen’s innovation is to argue that the most common initial condition is actually likely to resemble cold, empty space—not an obviously favorable starting point for the onset of inflation.

Recent research has shown that even empty space has faint traces of energy that fluctuate on the subatomic scale. Physicists Jaume Garriga and Alexander Vilenkin have suggested that these fluctuations can generate their own big bangs in tiny areas widely separated in time and space. Carroll and Chen take our universe, and others, to be such fluctuations in a high entropy multiverse.

On this view, while the initial state that produced our universe would appear to be, taken by itself, a highly improbable one, in the vastness of the multiverse the creation of our universe is not that unlikely. Indeed it is likely not even a unique event.

summaries.standard:
****Topic****

Starting conditions of the universe

****Framework****

Old/New

****Main Point****

Carroll and Chen are positing that the origins of our universe was a fluctuation of energy in cold, empty space, within a vast high entropy multiverse.

****Summary****

The first two paragraphs introduce some background information on the Big Bang inflationary period at the beginning of our universe, the view of C&C that this type of event isn't unique, and the emerging picture of the multiverse.

The third paragraph describes how C&C got to their view, via work on entropy, and then it explains what entropy is and provides an example.

The fourth paragraph brings together the two different threads: because of what we know about entropy, what we believe about the Big Bang seems like quite a mystery. The starting conditions for the Big Bang seem like extremely unlikely starting conditions. C&C's ****innovation**** (New) is saying that the most common starting condition would be cold, empty space.

The fifth paragraph, brings in the ****Recent**** (New) research of two other people, G&V, who are able to potentially explain how cold/empty space could give way to a fluctuation as big as the Big Bang.

The last paragraph ties it together: C&C think that our universe could have emerged from an energy fluctuation in cold, empty space, occurring in a high entropy multiverse, and they think this phenomenon would likely have occurred more than once.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately states the main idea of the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Supporting Text
explanationBlocks.body:
The central topic of this passage was the Big Bang. What about the Big Bang did the passage want us to know?

The main point of view is Carroll and Chen (C&C), who are saying ****the Big Bang was not unique****.

Within the 4th paragraph, we get more of the typical Old/New, Problem/Solution, Question/Answer framework we expect out of Science passages.

****OLD PROBLEM:****
Why was the initial condition for the Big Bang such a low entropy condition, given that high entropy conditions are way more common in the universe (so a random initial condition should be high entropy)

****NEW/RECENT SOLUTION:****
According to C&C, the most common random initial condition would be cold, empty space. And there's research saying that tiny fluctuations happen on the subatomic scale that may generate their own big bangs in tiny areas.

So the paradox is resolved by saying, "Yes, the initial condition should be high entropy ... and we're saying the Big Bang *did* start within a high entropy multiverse. It was only low entropy on a very local scale, because it arose out of a fluctuation of the subatomic scale, which is why it appears that the precursor to the Big Bang was small / hot / dense.

In these Old / New passages, we listen for the author's assessment at the very end, and the last paragraph sounds like he's curious and implicitly sympathetic to this point of view.

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body: Look for the proposed energy fluctuation in a high entropy multiverse. The vast scale makes an event likely to occur without making it frequent on ordinary timescales.

choices.text: Carroll and Chen theorize that our universe is the result of an energy fluctuation in a high entropy multiverse.
choices.explanation:
Since the Problem/Question was, "Given that high entropy is what we expect to be the default condition of the universe, why does it seem like the Big Bang came from some small/hot/dense low entropy precursor".

The researchers / the passage answer this question by saying, "Well it low entropy locally, in the subatomic pocket of space where the fluctuation occurred, but this was just a common blip in a high entropy multiverse".

choices.text: According to Carroll and Chen, entropy increases because there are more ways for a system to be disordered than for it to be ordered.
choices.explanation: This entropy principle is background supporting Carroll and Chen's proposal, not their central innovation. Attributing it to them does not contradict the passage merely because other physicists also accept it; its problem as a main point is narrow scope.

choices.text: Carroll and Chen challenge the prevailing view of physicists that our universe underwent a period of extremely rapid, massive inflation.
choices.explanation:
C&C aren't saying that the universe didn't undergo an inflationary stage. They're still upholding the possibility of inflation. They are just trying to resolve the question of why the ****pre****-inflationary universe seems low entropy.

They aren't changing the inflation part of the Big Bang story; they're just saying, "inflation (the Big Bang / aftermath) didn't come from some rare, unlikely low entropy universe, rather the Big Bang started in a low entropy subatomic patch of empty space, which was inside of a larger high entropy multiverse."

choices.text: According to Carroll and Chen, a small, hot, and dense configuration is unlikely as a random initial condition for a universe.
choices.explanation:
They would agree with this, but this is far too narrow. Their one sentence takeaway for us isn't, "Small / hot / dense is unlikely to be the random initial condition for a universe".

Their one sentence takeaway is "the Big Bang was probably just a relatively normal fluctuation that occurred in a tiny subatomic area of space within a high entropy multiverse".

choices.text: Carroll and Chen posit that our universe is one of many universes in an all-encompassing multiverse.
choices.explanation:
This is a pretty compelling second option. C&C would agree that our universe is one of potentially many in a big ol' multiverse.

But this answer is doing a poor job of addressing the central Problem/Question and C&C's innovative Solution/Answer.

The problem/question centered around the entropy paradox, so for this answer to not address the initial condition entropy problem is dodging the central issue of the passage.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following comes closest to capturing what the term “cosmic bubble” means in the last sentence of the second paragraph?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
We can picture our universe like a balloon, that was very small before it started inflating. (It is still inflating / expanding presently)

The idea of a multiverse is like a room full of balloons. Each balloon is its own universe. So the "cosmic bubble" means the barrier of our balloon.

We can't see other balloons because our entire universe's reality is trapped inside the cosmic bubble of its balloon.

choices.text: all-encompassing larger universe
choices.explanation: This answer matches the concept of the *multiverse*, the room full of balloons. The "cosmic bubble" just represents our ****smaller**** universe, the world within our balloon.

choices.text: universe contained in the multiverse
choices.explanation: This is referring to our balloon (the cosmic bubble of our universe), which is in a room full of balloons (other universes that together comprise the multiverse).

choices.text: inflation following a big bang
choices.explanation:
Our cosmic bubble did have a big bang, followed by a period of rapid inflation, mellowing out to today's slower rate of inflation.

But the cosmic bubble isn't the inflation itself. The balloon isn't the same thing as the first few breaths of air that go into the balloon.

The cosmic bubble is our observable universe, not a specific process that occurred after the Big Bang. This answer is probably trying to trap people with outside associations between "bubble" and "inflation".

choices.text: theoretical preconceptions
choices.explanation:
The "cosmic bubble" refers to our actual ****physical**** universe. Our theoretical ideas go beyond our cosmic bubble. After all, we invented a theoretical concept of a multiverse that exists outside our cosmic bubble.

We can't see other universes beyond our actual physical universe, because all observable things for us are within this physical boundaries of this cosmic bubble.

choices.text: low entropy state
choices.explanation:
This is just grabbing a buzzword from elsewhere in the passage. "Cosmic Bubble" is just a shorthand for our universe.

At some periods in its life, our universe may be in a low entropy state, but "low entropy state" isn't a synonym for "our universe".
